text:
Nigerian banks recorded stronger demand for consumer loans in the third quarter of 2026, with borrowing appetite among households rising alongside improved credit availability across secured, unsecured and corporate lending, a Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), survey has revealed.
The CBN’s Q3 2026 Credit Conditions Survey Report showed that demand for consumer loans to households rose to 42.9 index points during the quarter, while demand for house-purchase loans increased to 28 points.
The report, which was based on lenders’ responses in September, noted that “respondent banks reported increase in credit demand across secured credit (including all its lending types), unsecured (including all its types) and all corporate lending types in Q3 2026.”
The report showed that demand for overdrafts and personal loans to households also increased by 24.7 index points, while mortgage and remortgage lending rose by 12 points. However, demand for credit card lending declined by 20 index points, reflecting differing borrowing patterns across household credit products.
The report further showed that demand for secured lending increased by 25.6 index points, while unsecured and corporate lending recorded increases of 7.2 and 18.9 index points, respectively.
On the supply side, the CBN said, “Lenders indicated increase in overall credit availability in Q3 2026 across secured, unsecured and the corporate lending types.”
The survey recorded increases in credit availability indices of 5.5 points for secured lending, 18.9 points for unsecured credit and 24.3 points for corporate lending.
Explaining the factors behind the improvement, the report stated that the increase in secured credit availability was “largely driven by changing economic outlook, changing liquidity positions and market share objectives.”
For unsecured lending, it said the improvement was “primarily driven by market share objectives, changing economic outlook and changing cost/availability of funds.”
Similarly, the increase in corporate credit availability was “mainly attributed to changing appetite for risk, changing sector specific risks and market share objectives.”
Corporate borrowing demand was also driven by working capital requirements, with the report identifying inventory finance, which recorded 18.6 index points, as the leading contributor. Balance sheet restructuring and capital investments recorded 2.5 and 0.7 index points, respectively.
